analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal health programs from using quality-adjusted life years in coverage and payment decisions.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 211–208 on a strict party-line vote in February 2024, but the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal health programs would be barred from using quality-adjusted life years — a measure that rates the value of a year of life lower for someone who is elderly, disabled, or terminally ill — to decide what to cover or pay for. The ban would cover Medicare, Medicaid (including private managed-care plans), CHIP, and the federal employee health plan, and states could not waive it. The bill pays for itself by cutting the Affordable Care Act's Prevention and Public Health Fund from 2024 through 2029, and requires an annual government report on how quality-adjusted life years affect people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Disabled, elderly, and terminally ill patients in federal health programs gain a legal guarantee that their lives cannot be assigned a lower dollar value when coverage and payment thresholds are set — including in Medicaid managed-care plans and Medicare Advantage and Part D plans, where private insurers make utilization decisions. Brand-name drug makers also stand to gain, since value-assessment frameworks that price a treatment per quality-adjusted life year are a main tool for arguing that expensive drugs should be paid less or not covered at all; banning those measures in federal programs removes that pressure.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled patients on federal health programs

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits every federal health care program, including Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare Advantage, the Part D drug benefit, and the federal employee health plan, from using prices based on quality-adjusted life years — measures that discount the value of a life based on disability, age, or terminal illness — to set coverage, reimbursement, or incentive thresholds.

Extends the ban to Medicaid managed-care organizations, Medicare Advantage plans, and Part D prescription drug plans, so private insurers running those programs cannot use the measures in utilization decisions either.
Blocks federal agencies and states from waiving the ban through Medicaid or other demonstration and waiver authorities, closing a common route around statutory limits.

Requires the Government Accountability Office to report annually to Congress on how quality-adjusted life years negatively affect people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and their access to care.

analysis.who_pays: The Prevention and Public Health Fund, which funds community prevention, immunization, and chronic-disease programs, would be cut below its scheduled amounts for fiscal years 2024 through 2029 to offset the bill's cost. Federal and state health programs, and ultimately taxpayers, could also face higher costs if they lose cost-effectiveness tools for deciding what to pay for treatments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Community prevention and public health programs

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts the ACA Prevention and Public Health Fund for fiscal years 2024 through 2029, taking money from community prevention, immunization, and chronic-disease programs to pay for the QALY ban.

By barring quality-adjusted life years in every federal program, the bill removes a cost-effectiveness tool that economists and insurers use to judge whether a treatment's price is worth its benefit; removing it makes it harder to hold down drug prices and program spending, a trade-off an honest supporter has to acknowledge.

The ban applies very broadly — including to privately run Medicaid managed-care and Medicare plans — and critics argue such a sweeping prohibition could restrict plans' ability to make rational coverage choices, raising premiums and taxpayer costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection is real and aimed at a genuine problem: coverage formulas that implicitly value the lives of disabled, elderly, or terminally ill patients less. But the bill is blunt — it bans the measure everywhere in federal health care rather than regulating how it is used, which removes a tool for holding down drug prices, and it pays for the change by cutting prevention funding that mostly serves low-income communities. The benefit to patients is genuine but narrow in practice; the funding cut and the loss of cost-control leverage are immediate.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a near-party-line vote, but the Senate Finance Committee never took it up before the 118th Congress ended, so it died without ever getting a Senate vote.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 24, 2023 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees; the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee forwarded it by voice vote in March 2023.
The Energy and Commerce Committee ordered it reported as amended on a 27–20 vote on March 24, 2023, and it was reported on May 17, 2023.

The House took it up on February 7, 2024 under a rule reported February 5; a Democratic motion to recommit the bill failed 207–210, with all voting Democrats in favor and all voting Republicans opposed.
On final passage the House approved the bill 211–208 on February 7, 2024 — every vote in favor was a Republican and every vote against was a Democrat.
The Senate received the bill on February 8, 2024 and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which took no action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public health programs kept their funding, since the Prevention and Public Health Fund cut died with the bill, and Medicaid managed-care and Medicare plans kept their current decision-making tools. Brand-name drug makers also benefit from the bill's death, since value assessments based on quality-adjusted life years remain available to pressure high drug prices. Disabled patients, meanwhile, did not get the new legal protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public health programs and brand-name drug makers

sides.party_line_note: The vote split cleanly by party: all 211 yeas were Republicans and all 208 nays were Democrats, and the failed motion to recommit split the same way (207–210).

industries.note: Value-assessment frameworks that price a treatment per quality-adjusted life year are a principal tool for arguing that expensive drugs should be paid less. Banning those measures across every federal health program removes price pressure, so the bill would have locked in higher payments even while framed as patient protection.

industries.industry: Community prevention and public health programs
industries.note: The bill cuts the Prevention and Public Health Fund below scheduled levels for fiscal 2024–2029 to pay for the QALY ban, taking money from immunization and chronic-disease prevention efforts that largely serve ordinary communities. Because the bill died, the cut never happened.

industries.industry: Medicaid managed-care and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: The ban would extend to plans' own utilization decisions, limiting one tool they use to manage costs; in practice QALYs are used sparingly in U.S. programs, so the practical effect is small. Because the bill never became law, nothing changed for them.
